extracted.intended_audience: educated early-18th-century readers of The Spectator; general readers interested in literary criticism, manners, and morals
extracted.subtask_short: periodical essay on criticism and manners
extracted.subtask_description: A set of moral and literary prescriptions and observations presented as Spectator essays (Addison & Steele) about what constitutes good criticism, proper conduct in giving and charity, the role of fortune and prudence, and marriage finances. Written for a general, literate public.

rubrics_metrics.name: Critic's clarity and logical expression
rubrics_metrics.description: A critic must be able to think right and convey his Thoughts to another with Clearness and Perspicuity; mastery of logic is essential (Aristotle noted as both best Critick and best Logician).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Learn the art of distinguishing between Words and Things, range your Thoughts, and set them in proper Lights; without this an author or critic will lose himself in Confusion and Obscurity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Critic's learning and command of language
rubrics_metrics.description: A true critic should have good Insight into all the Parts of Learning and show mastery of the Elegance and Delicacy of his Native Tongue (as Greek and Latin critics do).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Familiarity with literature, classical authorities, and linguistic elegance is expected; critics who lack learning will betray themselves in phraseology and confused thought.

rubrics_metrics.name: Genuine scholarship versus superficial cant
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid setting up as a critic by mere adoption of a few general Rules or a cant of words drawn from fashionable sources (e.g., French authors); such mimicry enables illiterate heavy writers to pass as judicious.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Beware of superficial citations and fashionable jargon that mask lack of true learning—these are marks of an illiterate critic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Praise excellencies rather than dwell only on faults
rubrics_metrics.description: A true Critick ought to dwell rather upon Excellencies than Imperfections, to discover the concealed Beauties of a Writer, and communicate such things as are worth observation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not limit praise to passages already applauded by the public; seek hidden merits. As Dryden: 'He who would search for Pearls must dive below.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid ridicule and misplaced wit in criticism
rubrics_metrics.description: Mirth and ridicule are unseasonable in a critic when they prejudice the reader or make beauties the subject of derision; wit used in improper places is impertinent and absurd.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A man who cannot write with wit on a proper subject is dull; one who exerts it improperly attacks beauties and aggravates faults—criticism should be fair, not merely merry at an author's expense.

rubrics_metrics.name: Seriousness and instructiveness of manner
rubrics_metrics.description: The greatest masters, ancient and modern, in works of criticism have appeared with a serious and instructive Air; criticism should educate rather than mock.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopt a grave, instructive tone when instructing readers; pleasantry that substitutes for instruction is disingenuous.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proportionate treatment of great genius
rubrics_metrics.description: When discussing the works of a great genius, point out imperfections without endeavouring to inflame them with ridicule; productions of great genius with lapses are preferable to scrupulously exact works of inferior authors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Signal the ungrateful nature of certain critical tasks (e.g., pointing defects in Milton) and avoid unnecessary derision; Longinus's view of the sublime is invoked to temper judgment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Don't fix on trivial or already‑applauded faults
rubrics_metrics.description: One mark of a critic without taste is that he seldom praises anything not already received by the public, and that his criticism turns wholly upon little Faults and Errors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pointing out small blemishes that the public has already judged is easy but petty; critics should avoid merely collecting 'chaff' (Boccalini anecdote).

rubrics_metrics.name: Perform virtues with decency and becoming manner
rubrics_metrics.description: No man should be content that he barely does well; he should perform everything in the best and most becoming manner he is able—manner gives actions distinctive lustre.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Manner distinguishes similar actions (e.g., Mummius vs Carus in giving); strive for graceful, becoming behaviour so the act itself shines (examples from Titian, Pliny, classical exempla).

rubrics_metrics.name: Liberality must be cheerful and graceful
rubrics_metrics.description: Liberality should be performed with such Cheerfulness as may express the God-like Pleasure there is in obliging one's Fellow‑Creatures; the manner of bestowing adds to the gift.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Pliny's letter to Quintilian presents a gift made with care to avoid humiliating the receiver—the good grace of giving can double the obligation and soften the gift.

rubrics_metrics.name: Decorum augments moral authority and effectiveness
rubrics_metrics.description: Comeliness of Person and Decency of Behaviour add infinite Weight to what is pronounced by any one; lack of decency often makes rebukes and advice ineffective.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Graceful severity (youthful beauty rebuking the Devil in Milton), careful comportment at death (Cæsar, Lucretia) illustrate that decorum increases persuasive power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance prudence with openness to bold opportunity
rubrics_metrics.description: While a great part of good or ill Fortune arises from right or wrong measures (prudence), excessive caution may prevent great unforeseen successes; Fortune sometimes favours the young and the sanguine.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prudence usually produces success but can hinder extraordinary gains that come from risk; historical examples and maxims (Richelieu, Cicero, Timotheus) are cited to show nuance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Attribute success modestly; avoid arrogance
rubrics_metrics.description: It is a great Presumption to ascribe our Successes to our own management; one should esteem blessings as the Bounty of Heaven rather than solely personal acquisition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Humility before Providence is recommended; arrogance at ascribing all success to oneself displeases men of sense and (the author suggests) the Supreme Being.

rubrics_metrics.name: Support charitable institutions (charity‑schools)
rubrics_metrics.description: Charity‑schools are laudable institutions that clothe, feed, and instruct poor children, producing honest artificers and public benefit; benefactions to such schools are highly worthy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Benefits include moral and practical advantages: producing humble, religiously educated servants, preventing domestic slanders, and creating grateful, diligent dependents; the writer urges donations and transcribes Dr. Snape's praise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid separate purses and extravagant pin‑money in marriage
rubrics_metrics.description: The practice of pin‑money (a wife's separate allowance) is of late date and may furnish a wife with 'Arms against' her husband; separate purses between husband and wife are as unnatural as separate beds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The essay argues that pin‑money can inflame demands, encourage extravagant habits, and undermine marital unity; shared interests and joint finances are presented as preferable.
